utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing to delay us, could the witness be escorted in. But before -- usher, before he comes in -- Mr. Krgovic, continuing with the observation, I don't know I would put it as high as an objection that Ms. Korner raised yesterday, the Chamber would respectfully remind you that inasmuch as this witness has been called as an expert witness, and although in -- my recollection, and it may be a matter of the translation or interpretation that he -- that his explanation for some of the comments he made yesterday was based on his experience, that you should frame your questions in such a way that the witness is not blending, as it were, his observations out of which he is able to express an expert opinion from a broader, quote/unquote, experience, which may import any number of suppositions and things outside his realm of expertise. So if you would bear that in mind, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, General. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to begin, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday we commented on some of the paragraphs in your expert report. The last such paragraph was 51. You had explained already why it was only on the 12th of May that the decision on the setting up of the VRS was adopted. Please take a look at paragraph 52 in your report, where you say: [As read] "At the same session, a decision of the National Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina established the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The decision was adopted based on the constitution of Republika Srpska in response to the situation at the time and in accordance with the constitutional obligation of the National Assembly to 'regulate and ensure the defence and security of the Republic.'" You say "in response to the situation at the time." What did you have in mind when you chose that language?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I partly explained in my footnote. And yesterday, I pointed out the well-known fact that previously the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council had been established as two armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I meant when I wrote "the situation at the time." So I'm referring to the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was a situation of war or, actually, to be more precise, imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to take a look at footnote 16. And that's document 2D10 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab -- I apologise, I'll have to repeat the number. The document 2D100539.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I missed the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 16. Or, rather, footnote 16. I apologise, it's actually tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you hard copies of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The tab in your copy is 16, General. Page 2. General, this is the decision on the formation of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in Article 2, it says: "The existing Territorial Defence units and staffs shall be renamed as commands and units of the army whose organisation and establishment shall be determined by the president of the republic." General, please explain briefly of which units the Army of the RS consisted and what is the essence of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, and I can repeat now, that on the 4th of May, the federal leadership - and I mean that of Yugoslavia - adopted the decision on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina. After that, only TO units remained functional, and they had existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war, too, as in all other republics. We have seen that pursuant to a decision of the highest leadership of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence of BH had already been set up, and the situation was the same in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH was made up exclusively of units and staffs of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that a number of persons from the JNA joined the Army of the Republika Srpska? And when I say that, I mean people who hail from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the opinion that officers and non-commissioned officers, even soldiers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and were citizens of that republic, because all of us who lived in the Federation had a dual citizenship: A federal citizenship and a republican citizenship. And, thus, these persons had the opportunity to remain in the newly established Army of the Serbian Republic of BH. Of course, I can add those were times of great uncertainty. It was mostly left to the people to the decide themselves. Nobody knew what arrangements would be in place with regard to payment, accommodation, housing, and so on, so that a large part of officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina stayed in the Yugoslav People's Army which later become the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I am an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned that somewhat earlier the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been set up. Tell me, what kind of relationship was in place between the TO of the Serbian Republic of BH and the old TO, to call it that? Were there any changes, and how was that regulated?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the decision on the establishment of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of BH, or, rather, the reasoning of that decision, said that the units of Territorial Defence set up in the framework of the JNA remained in existence and remained functional. And these were newly established armed forces, to call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53, you say, General, that the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 15th of June, 1992, adopted the decision on the formation, organisation, establishment, and commanding of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which provided the foundation for the organisation of the army. In your binder, that's footnote 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we leaving this document? Mr. Krgovic? May I just ask, sorry, Your Honours. Because, Your Honours, the problem is it's apparently not part of the law library, and clearly the -- it was handed in for translation with this highlighting on it because the CLSS don't appear to be able to translate part of what is in Article 2 and I don't know how important it is. But they say, not surprisingly, illegible. So if it is to be exhibited, Mr. Krgovic, then I think we need a clean copy plus what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see what the Prosecutor means, but, to me, it is legible enough. Perhaps we can ask the General to read out the paragraph. And this will certainly be tendered so we can have it retranslated, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please take a look at paragraph 2 on the screen. Paragraph 2 of the decision of the setting up of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krgovic, but apart from what the witness's translation would be, the point that Ms. Korner is making is that if this is going to be tendered and/or migrated to the law library, these anomalies would have to be sorted out and how would you propose that that best be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will submit this document for retranslation. However, it is legible it. I can read it and I commented this very copy with the witness. But certainly we want to avoid this situation, a situation as with that document that Ms. Korner and I are arguing about. So it may be better for this one to be resubmitted for translation to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krgovic, I can read it, but I would like to remind the Bench that in paragraph 52 of my report, just before footnote 16, there is an quotation from that Article 2. And that quotation reads: [As read] "The existing Territorial Defence units and staffs shall be renamed as commands and units of the army, whose organisation and establishment shall be determined by the president of the Republic." I believe that you have a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the content of Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honours, I note at the very end it says that this -- this decision was published in the Official Gazette of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, so ... therefore, it should be in the law library already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That leapt out at me as well, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, absolutely, if it is in the law library already. We checked for this particular document, this particular document isn't, and then, therefore, it is in the law library, Mr. Krgovic needn't trouble to exhibit this or get it retranslated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of that fact, then I will not tender this document into evidence, provided it becomes part of the law library. But at any rate, I'm going to double-check this. I am particularly interested in these provisions whether it was incorporated in a law or published in a public gazette, but I don't think that this particular aspect is of much relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, could you please look at 65 ter document 003000D2, that's on our list. It's tab 11 in your binder, the footnote 17 B. And I think it is going to be much easier for you if you look for this particular footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise I will repeat. 00039D2, that's 65 ter number, or 2D100543.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm sorry to keep interrupting. But I don't see a footnote 17 B in the General's report and the document referred to in footnote 17 is not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are actually two documents mentioned in footnote 17. That's why I told the General what I told him, but this should be your tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, have you managed to find the decision on the forming of the commands?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's, rather, an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an order. General, can you tell us what implication does this order have in the process of the forming of an army?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is slightly unusual that nearly a month elapsed after the decision that we mentioned a minute ago to establish an army. And then one month later, an order is issued to form unit commands of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH, which, in fact, makes it possible to provide complete definition of the army, as well as its organisation, to have the army organised at both operative and tactical levels, to determine the number of corps and their strengths, to provide a legal frame for the civilian control over the army, to regulate the manner of takeover of weapons and equipment. In other words, everything that is necessary to be in place for an army to become functional and operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's a mistranslation of the date, if -- if what the General -- in English. It says the 18th of August, 1992. And I think the original does say "6."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I haven't noticed that. That's a mistranslation. And we're going to send this to the CLSS to correct it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was June. It wasn't August. Or maybe it's August. I can't see clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this enlarged in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is definitely June.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now move to the next page of your expert report; specifically paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also have paragraph 55 of the expert report in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read this portion where you say that: [As read] "The Army of Republika Srpska is defined as the armed force whose ... task is to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence and constitutional order of Republika Srpska." Can you please look at Exhibit 2D100565. That's footnote 20. And it's the same in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please, in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, the Law on the Army defines the role of the army. And it is defined as an armed force. What was the case with the police? In 1992, within the scope of the military doctrine or any other legal frame, was it ever defined as an armed force as well?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I particularly quoted this article of the law which reads that the Army of Republika Srpska is the only armed force whose tasks are to defend the sovereignty, territorial, independence and constitutional order of Republika Srpska as stipulated by the constitution. In other words, pursuant to this article, police or militia units or the Ministry of the Interior are not an integral part of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please repeat your answer because part of it hasn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted this Article of the Law on Defence, because it particularly emphasises that only the Army of Republika Srpska is defined as being an armed force whose task is to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence and constitutional order of Republika Srpska. Units and forces of the Ministry of Interior under this law do not constitute part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, before you go on, Mr. Krgovic. General, could you assist me with, in terms of your last answer, you say: "It particularly emphasises that only the Army of Republika Srpska is defined as being an armed force whose task," et cetera, the units and forces of the ministry do not constitute part of the armed forces. Could you assist me, please, with how you -- why do you say that? Because looking at Article 1, the way it reads is the Army of the Serbian Republic is an armed force defending the sovereignty, et cetera. I hear what you are saying, but could you explain to me why you deduce that it is that the army has the exclusive responsible for defending the territory, the sovereignty, et cetera. Looking at the words of Article 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the reason is because that was the practice in every country and that was the practice implemented in the former Yugoslavia. The armed forces were the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence. Militia had never been part of the armed forces. Those were units that are not trained to participate in combat operations. Police is intended to maintain primarily public law and order. For that reason, they are never incorporated into an armed forces. I don't know if this was of assistance to you. I mean, in terms of armed forces being involved in combat and war operations. And it is emphasised here that only the Army of Republika Srpska, they even left out the TO, because this army grew out of the merging of the former TO with the army. I -- I do agree that it is slightly complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, as a follow-up of the question posed to you by Mr. President, in paragraph 57 you say, and I'm going to paraphrase, that subsequent laws from 1994, units of the MUP were envisaged to be a part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But that took place only in 1994. I don't know the genuine reasons for making such a decision, but I think that is rather unusual for the police to become part of an armed force. However, the then-leadership of Republika Srpska probably had their own reasons that guided them to take such a decision. But a minute ago, I was speaking about 1992, at the time when the army was formed, and that, at that time, the army was the only armed force, and that draws a clear line between them, on the one hand, and paramilitary units and the police on the other. Of course, I am not equating the police units and paramilitary formations. I'm just trying to make the distinction between the notion of armed forces on the one hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at paragraph 56, where you speak about and quote the Law on Defence. Can you please look at a document, 2D100567. This is your footnote 21. I believe it's tab 14 on the Defence list, the Zupljanin Defence list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm a little bit confused here. Tab 14, what is -- what is that document number referring to? 2D100567?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's 2D100567. And the 65 ter number is 00041D2; that's the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the 2D number is -- what number, is that, an ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the doc ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at Article 10. Here, in paragraph 56, you discuss the remit of the Ministry of the Interior in the sphere of defence. You say that the Law on Defence regulated the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Interior. Under the law, who is it who decides about the use of police in wartime operations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of the police in combat operations can be ordered exclusively by the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 56, you also say that, in practice, police units of the RS MUP participated in the execution of combat tasks, either jointly with the VRS or resubordinated to it. Can you explain what you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, first and foremost, wanted to point out the difference between practice and theory. To the extent I was able to draw conclusions from the documents I analysed, there were two ways of using the police in combat operations. One way, which, to my mind, was more correct, was the following. The army informed the CSB and requested a certain number of units, or a certain number of men, to be attached to army units, and then police units would act -- would act in coordinated actions with units of the VRS. But I was able to see in some documents that there were other ways, too; namely, that local commanders, on their own, decided to resubordinate police units of on the ground. To my mind, that manner of using police units of is less correct. That is why I wanted to point out this difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Having mentioned these two alternatives, what is the relationship between the police units and the VRS, in either case?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is actually the gist of it. Let's now leave aside how police units were used. In both cases, they were subordinated to the commander, the military commander, seeking to accomplish a military mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In footnote 22, you cite a document which I'm going to show you now. The document number is 1D00406. And that's footnote 22 in your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The tab number is 15 for everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, please take a look at this document. At the beginning, you see a statement of reasons why the -- why the order is issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the third paragraph from the bottom; that is, the third and the fourth. It says here that: "The exclusive right to command and use a unit is with the zone commander." And it goes on to say: [As read] "In the conduct of combat activities, all police forces shall be placed under the command of the zone commander who shall decide how they are used." Now we can go back to the first document which is titled: "Determining Zones of Responsibility." Could you comment on this document with regard to the delimitation of zones and the commanding of zones?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, within his jurisdiction and remit, has the right to issue orders and establish zones of responsibility in accordance with his assessment of the situation on the ground and the carrying out of combat operations. In his order, the commander must precisely delimit the zones, state who was in command there, and define their respective tasks. It also follows from that document that the commander orders police units to be placed under the command of the zone commander in order to carry out combat tasks. That is possible in certain situations, but it should be an exception rather than a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Must these newly established zones match the zone of responsibility of brigades?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't. These provisional zones are a result of the assessment of the situation on the ground, as well as the nature of the combat task to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the two manners of using police units. What about this case? Which manner of use of the police would this be?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke conditionally --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, at the moment, what's happening is the translation is running behind. The General starts answering before we get the translation of your question. So I wonder if you could try and leave a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, we have a problem with interpretation. The two of us speak the same language and I tend to speak fast, so please allow for a short pause before you begin answering. Possibly my question was a bit unclear too, so I'll repeat. You spoke about the two manners and you explained why you used those two terms. In one case, they are resubordinated directly without a decision or approval; and in the alternative case, there was a procedure in place. In this specific example, which of the two applies?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to give a precise answer to your question only based on this document. Possibly the corps commander was authorised by the commander of the Main Staff, and he, in turn, by the president of the republic, whom I mentioned a short while ago as the only one who had the right to decide about the use of police forces in combat. In this case, we do not know if the commander was so authorised or made the decision independently, based on his assessment of the situation and the threat in certain zones. That is, the threat posed to the population and property, and, as commander, he has the right to command all units in his zone of responsibility. But I would like to point out that, in this case, it isn't so important. What's key and what you asked me is the following: The commander made a decision. The units became part of the military, and by that very fact, they were subordinated to the commander of the military unit. That is much more important than the way how they ever got to be part of the military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just one moment. Mr. Witness, you say "the units became part of the military ..." May I ask you which units? I mean, are these all units within a certain territory; or were these particular units that had been assigned, as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document that we're discussing now, we read only during the execution of combat operations all police forces are placed under the command of the zone commander who decides about their use. So it says very clearly: All police forces. What exactly that is or how strong these forces are, I cannot say, because I wasn't there. It is it important to underline, Your Honours that there is no parallel command in an army. You can't have two persons issuing orders and commands. There can only be one person in charge. There is no collective command responsibility or responsibility in general. And that is why it is always said that whatever is incorporated into the army, it has to be subordinated to the person who had been appointed to that very position by a state organ and act as a brigade commander, a corps commander, or a division commander. And the virtue of this appointment gives him this authority. All the forces that are part of his units are subordinated to him. However, in the course of carrying out peacetime or wartime assignments, he is in -- allowed to delegate his responsibility and authority to lower officers. However, his personal responsibility cannot be delegated to anyone because it is inherent to his function and his post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, Mr. Kovacevic, but my concern is this: This all relates to a certain territory, I suppose. Can you define the territory to which it pertains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, the zone boundaries are precisely defined of that territory. For example, on page 1, paragraph 1, it says that: [As read] "The commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade shall be responsible for organising and carrying out combat activities in the zone." And then we have a list of names, Dubica, Sanski Most, Sanica and Ivanjska village. And all the troops deployed in that area which might cover some 50 kilometres, let's say, are subordinated to this particular commander in carrying out combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, then, during that time, if all police units are subordinated to the -- to the military and are part of the army, who is doing the police work then? In that zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked myself the same question when I was reading these documents and drafting my report, because it's simply inconceivable; but, on the other hand, it is hard to understand a lot of things during a war. If you don't have enough men to cover certain front line, I suppose that the easiest way out of that situation is to engage police units who bear arms and who have some level of military training. I suppose that the commanders had no choice but to act in that way, which, on the other hand, left the chiefs of the CSBs without their forces. And you are right about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, as a follow-up of the question asked of you by the Judge, here, we have a clear definition of areas of responsibility. Now, what happened when you have resubordination of police units without zones of responsibility being defined but they are, rather, sent to a brigade? What are the responsibilities of the brigade commander in that particular instance?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to give you a general answer to that. We would have to analyse how it worked on the grouped. And I can only talk about what I found in the documents. Similarly, if a brigade commander is assigned a specific task and if some of his axes or his front lines was in danger, he will definitely order the use of the most adjacent police force. But I'm telling you that those should have been exceptions, according to my experience and according to the military practice. I don't think that this should have happened thus often. I'm sorry. My brother is a police officer, for example. He was a police officer during the war. He lives in Prnjavor. And as a policeman, he was sent out to carry out combat assignments 300 kilometres from his police station, which, to me, doesn't sound very logical. And that happened quite a few times during the war, and I discussed these matters with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back now to your expert report. In paragraph 58, you say that the organisation of the VRS was outlined after its formation. And you also say that the policies and the doctrine of the defence of Republika Srpska, which were supposed to serve as the basis for the organisation of the army were not defined. Can you tell us whether, in general, the Law on Army envisaged a sort of -- its general role, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, its general role was, indeed, defined, and that is what I spoke about a minute ago, and I'm going to repeat it now. The task of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order of Republika Srpska. However, basically, each army has only two tasks. In peacetime, its task is to maintain a high level of combat readiness, or, as they call it in the west, operative capacity; whereas in wartime, its basic task is to defeat the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 59 - can you please take a look at it - you say that the organisation resembled that of the former JNA with due respect for certain specific features. Then you went onto say that - and that's in paragraph 63 - that was the so-called "line-staff type of organisation." When you say "line-staff," you explain some of the principles that pertain to it. However, can you explain to us in more detail this principle of line-staff type? Can you simplify it a little bit for us because this is rather complicated military terminology.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, I partly answered that question when I spoke about the commander having the sole right to command. It might be better for me to explain this, although the Honourable Chamber is aware of that, but I will say that every system and every state, in order to improve its functioning, relies on two social functions. The first one is government which exists in every country and every system. There is somebody who governs the country and takes decisions. And another social function is management or execution which is responsible for putting those decisions into practice. And there's another -- a third social function which is called command. However, it is characteristics of one system alone, and that system is called an army. And that applies to every single army. Why is that the case? It would take too much time for me to explain, but I would just say that the essence of the army defines its position. Army has to deal with a large number of human beings with enormous amounts of lethal weapons, and I'm sure that this third aspect was introduced only in the army and partially it exists within the police. This command function relies on singleness of command and subordination; that is to say, the right of commanders to command. When we tried to explain this principle to our cadets, we always say that all those functions that begin with a K in the Serbian language, means commander, commands, brigade commander, et cetera; whereas, all the other functions that end with a K in the Serbian language, such as chief, assistant, those are the people who are managing or controlling or assisting the process. So the exclusive right of command which is something that coincides with this line of chain of command that goes from the president downwards to the last private on the ground, via all the commanders, such as brigade commanders, company commander, et cetera, follows this line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about this chain of command, you said that the positions that end with a K are not entitled to command. What about the president? It also ends with a K.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The word president, such as president of the Parliament or the prime minister, have an executive function. But the president of a state always has a phrase Commander-in-Chief after his title, which gives him this right to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to move to another topic so I think this is maybe a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to your report. In paragraph 59 which is before you, you discuss the VRS. Did you also provide a schematic on the same page depicting the command structure of the VRS? There, we can see that the Supreme Commander is the president of the republic. In keeping with his scope of authority, could the president delegate the right of command to someone else, and who?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the republic can delegate part of his responsibility for commanding the army, and I believe it was, indeed, done during the war. Part of his responsibilities was delegated to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. There are several documents confirming this. Occasionally, I would come across a document which the end would say the Commander of the Main Staff is hereby authorised to deal with the specifics of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you also provide a detailed structure of the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There seems to be a part of the transcript missing. Could you repeat the last sentence. You said you viewed a number of documents and then ... please repeat that part.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When drafting this report, in order to corroborate a previous assertion I made, I can say that I came across certain documents where one finds that the president of the republic is authorising the commander of the Main Staff to regulate certain specific issues related to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 66, you discuss the structure of the VRS. You also say that the competences of the different organs at different levels of command is something that the VRS has not worked out, but it did rely on the existing orders and regulations pertaining to the units of the JNA. In footnote 31, you refer to regulations on the responsibilities of the Land Army Corps Command in peacetime. Please, let's look at the document you refer to. It's 65 ter 0097D2, if I'm not mistaken. Sorry, 47. Tab 23 for the other participants. When you discuss the documents used by the VRS, I believe you had this document in mind, as well as a number of others. In addition to the book of rules on the responsibilities of the grounds forces corps command in peacetime, do you know what other documents were used by the VRS and at what level of command? And I have in mind the strategic, operational, and tactical level. Were such documents used at all levels, since, here, you only refer to a single book of rules. That, I guess, would be my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not objecting to the question provided the General gives the basis for saying why he knows that the book of rules on the responsibilities of ground forces corps command in peacetime were those used by the VRS at a time of a state of war, or imminent war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to assist concerning the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I don't think Mr. Krgovic should assist the General. I think the General should answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you can ask him that in cross-examination. You put forth your objection, and you're free to put your own questions later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, unless the General does explain the basis, because it is not set out in his report, I do object to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, a question: When drafting your report, did you come across any rules about the competencies of the command of the land army in the VRS? And I have in mind 1992.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't come across such a document. From personal experience, I can say that it was a time of war. The army was established and organised. The establishment system was set up. And, as I mention in the report, the organisational principles used resembled, to a great extent, the ones used in the JNA. Due to the conditions that prevailed and shortness of time, this was done in such a way. There was no need to do anything else because these books of rules, which were produced in peacetime, pertaining to the JNA, envisaged even such situations, and I used this example of the rules of the Land Army Corps Command in peacetime. It was but one example of rules used in the JNA, much as it was used in the VRS. We have clear definitions of the competencies of all levels of command within, in this case, the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, based on your experience and work at the Military Academy, can you tell us what was the situation like, in terms of applying JNA rules to other armed forces in the region?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the other armed forces of the region also partially relied on the rules and regulations of the former JNA. I said already - yesterday, I believe - that everyone made use of what they deemed fit. I need to remind everyone that the JNA was a respectable armed force and that the rules and documents used by it were, for the most part, compatible or similar to similar such rules in existence in the other armed forces of Europe and elsewhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of command and control of armed forces, you dedicate part of your report to the Armed Forces of the FRY. I won't go in much detail in that part. I just wanted to ask you this: What is the relationship between the system of command and control in the Armed Forces of the SFRY, and here I mean the principles used, with the system of command and control in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago I was trying to explain the difference between control, command, and monitoring. I precisely stated that command is only present in the system or organisation that we refer to as the army. It always has its foundation in the principle of singleness of command and subordination, relying on the relationship between a superior and a subordinate. In each situation, it is always known who the commander is, who makes the decisions, and the subordinate must implement the superior's decisions, unless they contravene international humanitarian law. This is not the principle that was only followed by the JNA. At the helm of each and every armed forces, we have the president of the state, then the commander of the Main Staff, and, further down, commander of the corps, brigade, et cetera, all the way down to the single private. In terms of your question of command and control in the JNA, I can only tell you that the same principles were used by the VRS, and I'm certain such rules were also used by the other armed forces created in territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when providing such lengthy answers, please slow down, as the interpreters have to catch up. Do not forget that everything we say is being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 112. Paragraph 112 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There you say that when issuing an order, the superior in question was obliged to ensure that it was realistic and could be executed. Is the superior also obliged to keep in mind other regulation and rules in addition to this strictly narrow military interpretation of such rules?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. A moment ago I said that the superior makes decisions and issues orders, and the subordinates are duty-bound to implement them. I state here that the superior is obliged to ensure that such decisions are realistic and could be executed. In other words, it means that he needs to be well acquainted with his unit, the situation it is in, as well as the situation in the field. Having all that in mind, he sets tasks that can be executed. It is possible -- or, actually, not only possible but I believe here I should also have said that what the superior was obliged to ensure was that it is realistic, could be executed, and that it is legal, since, as we all know, there were violations of the international laws of war in this war, much as in all other wars. This is the word I suppose is missing. The legality is always understood and taken as something that is granted but, nevertheless, it should always be borne in mind when a superior makes decisions or issues orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your report, when you discuss the principles of command and control, in paragraphs 127 and further, you discuss responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at paragraph 127, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 133, 134, and 135, you discuss one's responsibility for the acts of one's subordinates. You say that a superior officer is personally responsible for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that his subordinates or other units or individuals prepared for such violations. He is also responsible for not taking measures if informed in a timely manner for failing to prevent them from committing such acts. Does this specific type of responsibility refer to all subordinate units under a single commander?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before the General answers, if Mr. Krgovic is reading out paragraph 134, it's been translated as: A superior officer is personally responsible for the violation of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that his subordinates or other units or individuals prepared for such violations. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not how it's been translated in the English. But that's -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This paragraph, 134, which you have just read out, is, in its entirety, a quotation from the regulation about the application of the provisions of international laws of war in the Armed Forces of the then-SFRY. As you know, Yugoslavia was a signatory to all international conventions and undertook to honour all these rules. I can answer your question unambiguously. The superior officer is responsible for any violation of the international law of war by his subordinates under the condition that he was aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 135, we read: [As read] "A military officer is also personally responsible if he knows that violations of the laws of war were committed but fails to take disciplinary or criminal action against the perpetrator, or, does not report the perpetrator to the competent military officer if he is not competent for taking action." General, this somewhat widens the obligation to instigate proceedings and, in addition, we learned that a military officer is personal [as interpreted] if he fails to report the perpetrators. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, too, is a provision from the regulations that I have quoted. In this specific case, if an individual learns of any violation of the international laws of war and is not competent - that was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: - then it is possible that the individual who violated the international laws of war does not belong to his units, or is not under his command. Due to that fact, the officer is not competent to take action, but he must report such an individual to such a person who is competent to take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This obligation of the military officer, with regard to violations of the international laws of war, does it also apply to resubordinated units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. When I spoke about competencies, I said that the officer was not -- or didn't have competence with regard to persons who are not members of his units. But when we speak about resubordinated units, then that is the case. The relationship, superior/subordinate, is in place, and, in that case, the superior officer is competent to take action against individuals who violated the international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does that also apply to the competence to instigate disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. All types of responsibility, from moral, through disciplinary, to criminal. In a word, the superior officer has the right to take action against individuals who are members of his units or attached units or resubordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at the section of your report that begins with paragraph 147. In this section, you elaborate on the "command (line)" relations in command and control. In paragraph 150, you speak about the relationship between superiors and subordinates, and with regard to rank or class and position, juniors and seniors. You provided a partial answer yesterday, but I would like you to expand on these terms that you mention in paragraph 150.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship between a superior and a subordinate is the basic and dominant relationship in any army. It is regulated by the organisation and the establishment or the order appointing a certain officer to a position. And, if pursuant to an order issued by the president of the republic or the commander of the Main Staff, somebody is appointed brigade commander, for example, then, he is the superior officer of all officers, soldiers, and civilian serving in that brigade. This is the superior/subordinate relationship. However, there's also military education, there's also promotion in the army, and that is mostly done through the system of ranks. When I spoke about officers, you get the first officer's rank when you graduate from Military Academy and you get your first star. And when we talk about ranks, there is the junior/senior relationship. After some time in the army, you are promoted to a higher rank. From second lieutenant, you become lieutenant, and then captain. And then you have to complete some course in order to become major, and after additional courses or training you become lieutenant-colonel, and so on. So it is clear who is junior and who is senior. But the one who is at the head of a unit is always in command, irrespective of his rank at any given moment. In practice, there have been exceptions, however rare, that the officer commanding a unit had a lower rank than -- of another officer in that unit. That was very rare but it is possible. That all goes hand in hand with some entitlements. An officer with a higher rank has a higher salary, but then there are also some entitlements that go with the position, and that -- these are also reflected in the income and so on. We soldiers certainly have no problems with understanding who is a superior and who is a subordinate. But I can provide additional explanation, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, further on in your report, you also dealt with the notions of decision and order. So let us go to paragraph 163. We see in paragraphs 162 and 163 your explanations of the essence, or the essential elements of orders. And you state that the essential part of an order, or the key element, is the commander's decision. And further down, in paragraphs 164 and 165, you outline the contents of a decision. I'm specifically interested in the part of paragraph 165, where you state the contents of a decision. The conceptual part of the decision, the type of operation, combat action. I needn't read on. And then you say basics of coordinated action and co-operation and combat readiness. Could you please elaborate, General, on the contents of a decision and what stems from it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As is stated here, the decision is the most important part and the key element of any commander's order. It is also the most difficult part. For example, when a situation changes, all the organs of a command, if there is time, gather; if not, then the commander, within the inner circle of the command, or sometimes even alone, considers the situation, makes an assessment of the enemy and your own forces, the situation in the territory, and the elements of time and space. And based on all that, including the suggestions of the individual organs, if present, the commander makes a decision which includes the parts that you have read out: Type of operation, combat action, objective of operation, the concept of manoeuvre, the classification of tasks into immediate and subsequent, manner of engagement, basis for coordinated action and collaboration and combat readiness, tasks and reinforcements for subordinate units, composition and tasks of support units, composition tasks of the reserve, basic organisation of combat operations support, and so on. So these are the mandatory elements of a decision, the mandatory theoretical elements. In practice, of course, not each and every element must be present always. It depends on the task, the forces at your disposal, the units at your disposal. If you lack anti-armour equipment, then, of course, you won't include that. If you have no anti-aircraft armaments then you won't take that into consideration. If there is no coordinated action, then you won't mention it. But these are the mandatory elements of a decision. And often commanders who want to show that they were attentive in college, they mention such elements as make sure [as interpreted] that there's coordinated action and co-operation, although in that specific task, there is no coordinated action or co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When a coordinated action and co-operation is being planned, is it necessary to adopt a plan to that effect or to further elaborate the issue?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before taking a decision on a coordinated action, there is a so-called coordination or synchronisation, as it is dubbed in the west, which entails the drawing up a plan of operation as a broader document which contains the tasks of individual elements or units participating in the implementation of a specific tasks. Provided there is time, and if it is possible, the commander or his deputy, along with a number of officers who play key roles in the execution of that task, carry out commander's reconnaissance in order to make sure that this plan of coordination fits the reality on the ground. Based on this coordination plan as a broader document, a plan of coordinated action is drawn up which includes provisions as to who, with whom, and with how many troops is going to take part in a coordinated action. It gives spatial and temporal designations, and it also specifies which units are going to be involved. This is another document that must be made as part of combat operations plan, again, is a broader document than the first two: The plan of coordination and the plan of a coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, further on, you dealt with the issue of combat documents in paragraph 173. These documents serve for the implementation of the commander's decisions. Now my question is: In the course of carrying out a combat task, and in view of the commander's decision to do so, is there any co-operation that exists there? Or does the implementation of the decision of the commander receive a different treatment?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander's decision is materialised by way of combat documents that I talk about in paragraph 173. It is made in writing and distributed to the relevant units by means of an order. In most cases, these documents must be acted upon without fail. Now, let me tell you that I didn't quite understand your question. And why are you talking about co-operation? There is no co-operation once a commander takes a decision. Coordination may exist during the preparation of a decision between individual organs of the command until the stage is reached when a decision is made.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Co-operation may exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once a decision is made, converted into writing, and conveyed to the unit, it has to be carried out except if it is in contravention of a law. However, in the course of the implementation of this decision and the combat task, it is possible within the framework and the contents of the task to have a certain form the co-operation between the unit implementing the commander's decision and other authorities on the ground. And that is the only instance when we can speak about co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you also dealt in your report with command and control of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska from paragraph 175 onwards. And, here, you put forth certain conclusions that you, yourself, reached. However, I'm not going to ask you about it because we commented this portion of your report earlier. Now, let us go to paragraph 188 of your report. Here, you speak about those who were responsible for operational command and the responsibilities of the commander of the Main Staff. So could you please look at footnote 93, which is 65 ter 001 -- 0081D2, and for other parties that's tab 59 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. If you look at Article 175 of the Law ... A while ago, you spoke about the powers of the president and the delegation of powers. Can you briefly comment on this Article 175 and compare it to the corresponding paragraph in your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president is, indeed, the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, but the president cannot exercise command over the army on a daily basis. This is not the idea. So the powers of the president are also defined by the constitution and the Law on Defence. The president decides on the state of war, declares an imminent threat of war, et cetera, et cetera. However, daily command of the army, the use of the army, and the resolving all other solutions -- all other issues are delegated by the president to the commander of the Main Staff. And that is in line with the provisions contained in Article 175 of the Law on Defence, I think. Due to that, I quoted this paragraph in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, further on in your report, starting from 191, you speak about command and control of the VRS. Can you tell us, is there a parallel between the regulations and the practice with the practice of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we speak about theoretical frameworks and some basic principles of command, I already said that there was no difference whatsoever. Here, as well, it is also known who is on the top of the pyramid and who is at the bottom. Here we have the president of the republic at the helm, as Commander-in-Chief, as was the case previously in the JNA. In other words, the principles and the responsibilities, the command relations, the line relations, the reporting principles from subordinates to superiors, the principle of sending information from subordinate -- from superior to subordinate, all of this was implemented in practice but it was adapted to the conditions of an imminent threat of war, or maybe we should say a state of war. I'm sorry. Of course, there are some competencies here that were expanded, but that was also envisaged by the rules and regulations of the Yugoslav People's Army. Because, here, you have a wide range of members of the reserve forces who are now members of the army because they were mobilised in a state of war or an imminent state of war. There is also mention of the establishment of military courts and Military Prosecutor's offices and all other issues that are always part of an imminent threat of war. However, when it comes to command and control, I don't think that there were any major differences in the principles that were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, now that you mentioned an imminent threat of war and the declaration of a state of war, when we talk about the powers and responsibilities of unit commanders - I'm talking about the brigade and corps commanders - is there any difference between their competencies and responsibilities during an imminent threat of war and a declared state of war, whilst they're engaged in carrying out combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, there is no major difference between a state of imminent threat of war and a state of war when we talk about the competencies and responsibilities of both superiors and subordinates. The only difference is, if I may say so, psychological because we soldiers know what an imminent threat of war is. The very notion is self-explanatory, it says that it is something that precedes a war, and it's a state that cannot last perpetuate, can only last for a month or two or three, once you realise that there is danger of war. However, once a war is declared and then it lasts for three, four, or five years, then soldier [as interpreted] don't understand why it was not declared a war. Although I'm not a expert in legal matters and I'm doing my best to understand them as much as I can, I can deduce that in terms of competencies and responsibilities, there were no substantial differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 193, you speak about the line or the chain of command. And you say that: "No persons other than commanders ... were ever part of the chain of command at any level ..." And in paragraph 194, you say that: "The line of reporting goes in the opposite direction." Please explain the line of reporting and the chain of command from the aspect of the VRS. Yesterday when you mentioned some examples from practice, you were referring to the JNA. So I'm interested in these two relationships. Perhaps it's possible to interpret them in connection.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained how a commander makes a decision and how that decision is implemented. Here, the chain of command goes from the superior to the subordinate. That's how the implementation of the commander's decision proceeds. It is the same in the VRS as in the former JNA. The same principle applies. But the line of reporting goes in the opposite direction, from the subordinates, from the lowest-ranking units, toward the superiors. For example, every commander, and in the lowest level in the VRS was the squad commander, then through the platoon commander, the company commander, the battalion commander, and so on upwards, all these were duty-bound, as provided for by the rules and regulations, to submit daily reports about the events during the day or how they implemented their tasks. Certainly these reports grew ever longer, as they went up the chain. Sometimes reports were oral, either submitted personally or over the phone, and then, from a certain level, they had to be in writing, and it all depended on the situation in the battlefield. But, certainly, the line of reporting goes bottoms up. I mentioned another line, and that's the line of information. So in order to avoid confusion, it's the subordinates who are duty-bound to report. And when these reports are received at a higher level - at the Main Staff or at the corps command - then, according to the theory and the rules and regulations, they must be analysed for the previous day or the previous week. Then a integrated report is compiled upon which the superior informs his subordinates. So the subordinates report to the superior, and the superior informs the subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic has just informed me that your words have not been adequately interpreted. Could you please explain this difference between reporting and information.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line of reporting goes from the subordinates to the superiors, from the lowest levels of military organisation towards the highest forms of military organisation. These subordinates are duty-bound to report daily to the superior command about the implementation of the commander's decision. When these reports are received at a certain level of command, they are analysed during the day, a summary report about the most important events is compiled, and then these higher levels inform the subordinate levels about the contents, positive or negative, about the need to take additional measures or whatever. So let me repeat: The line of reporting goes from the lower levels to the upper levels; whereas, the line of information goes from the upper levels to the lower levels. However, the chain of command is always the same. It goes from the upper levels to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 195, you say: "All of the above that pertain to the commanding function and the chain of command also pertains to temporary formations and resubordinated units." Could you explain, in a nutshell, which commanding functions you mean that also pertain to temporary formations and resubordinated units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be read in connection with what is said in the immediately preceding paragraphs: The function of reporting and the function of information. All that is said about that also applies to temporary formations and resubordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does the principle of command, singleness of command, also apply to temporary functions and resubordinated units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have repeated that more than once. Any unit that is incorporated into the -- into the units that you command becomes part of your establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point, Mr. Krgovic? So we take the break to return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we finished this part that contains paragraph 195. And in the following paragraphs, you discuss responsibility. When answering some of my questions, you pointed out the link. Let us move onto the section of your report that begins with paragraph 207 and the chapter heading is: "Resubordination and Coordination." In paragraph 207, you list some terms: Recruitment, resubordination, attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation. Before we start analysing your report in more detail, could you please explain in simple terms what these terms I have read out mean, or point out the distinction between their respective meanings and that of resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this section of my work, I insist on the terms you mentioned. That is because, to my mind, with regard to the character of the indictment and the assignment I was given, these terms, apart from the term of command that has been discussed at great length, are very important, and they must be explained to the Trial Chamber with precision. This is what I'm about to do now. These terms designate some actions that are taken in order for the commander's decision - mentioned before - to be implemented as efficient -- as efficiently and fully as possible. Recruitment is the initial action. To do something, you must recruit personnel. It is regulated through laws and regulations how units are -- how units are manned by personnel to carry out its tasks. Take a given unit. If you're its commander, for example, brigade commander, then what is under your jurisdiction is something that can you resubordinate during the execution of combat operations. In other words, you can execute this action of resubordination. What does that mean? A lower-ranking unit, and it's always a lower-ranking unit, so I give the example of a brigade commander, he can take a company from one battalion and resubordinate that company to another commander because that company is one of his own units, and that's how he goes about it. Takes a company from one commander and gives it to another for this other to use in order to accomplish a certain mission. That is the action described by that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, if I might interrupt the witness as he goes forward. General, looking at the opening portion of paragraph 207, where you say, "Taking into account the importance of this topic and certain disagreements," and you go on, as you go forward with your answer's to Mr. Krgovic's question, I'm not sure that I understand to what extent you're using these terms as they were generally or broadly understood as contrasted with how you choose for your own purposes to use the terms. Do you get the distinction that I'm asking you to clarify for me? Because you -- you -- you -- you say, that there are contradictions in the theoretical concepts, and I'm wondering whether the way that -- sorry, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours I'm not sure that's what he means. I rather feel he is being given information. He doesn't explain it but I think he has been given information about this case. So I'm not sure that is he talking about theoretical concepts by using those words: "Taking into account the importance of this topic and certain disagreements ..." Your Honours may want to clarify that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank -- thank -- thank you, Ms. Korner. I ... Let's proceed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, with regard to this introduction of yours about making a distinction due to certain disagreements and contradictions and theoretical legal documents, can you point out these contradictions and show how they are linked with the importance of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I, myself, haven't really understood. When you mention contradictions, are you referring to a general theory or this specific case? This is the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was chief of the Military Academy, which is a known fact. I first attended that school as a student, and I listened to what my teachers had to say and also read the textbooks explaining these terms. This is partly what I had in mind because, in some textbooks, it is very difficult to see the distinction between attachment and resubordination. And bearing in mind that, in this case, the use of units in combat operations is an important topic, in theory, as I said, few explanations can be found, so that, to my mind, these units are actually attached to military units. I've already said that resubordination exists when you resubordinate something that you have anyway. But when somebody else gives you something, and that somebody else can be a superior commander, then that something you're given isn't really yours. It doesn't belong to you. And we cannot speak of -- then we speak about attachment. However, the relationship between superior and subordinate is always in place. There is something of a confusion present in theory, and I believe I can claim that with full authority, and I have also mentioned this as a problem to some theoreticians that these terms must be better defined in our theory, I mean, Serbian theory. So you can resubordinate something that is yours, and if it is not yours, then it's attachment. But certainly whenever you receive something as a commander, then the relationship, superior/subordinate is in place. When you carry out some action, be it attachment or resubordination, the relationship between superior and subordinate is always in place. I don't know if I was clear enough. And this is why I mentioned this in my introduction, especially due to the fact that there has been dual practice here when it comes to the use of police in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, can I put, then, a clarifying question to you. What if you're not resubordinating a unit that belongs to you, but you're, rather, claiming a unit from another authority. That is to say that you're claiming a unit that does not belong to you, and as a consequence of your claim you receive that unit and put it into your own jurisdiction. What is that, in your view? Is that resubordination, or is it attachment, or is it something else? Because in the examples that we have discussed at some length in this trial, the understanding was that the army commander could claim to have police units transferred to his command for particular purposes and for a limited period of time, and at least I have been led to believe that this is what, in military terms, would be called resubordination. However, this does in the fit with the definition that you have just offered. So now I don't know where to settle my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be even clearer. I understand your question. This is precisely what I tried to stress. In both instances, the relationship, superior/subordinate, is present. Even if you receive such a unit, as you say, by virtue of that act, it is being resubordinated to the commander in charge of the task. There is no double command or parallel chain of command. To repeat: In our theory, there are these two terms which I tried to distinguish. If a commander has his own unit, he can also move parts of that unit around, and that's where the difference is between attachment and resubordination. In any case, if you receive a unit or if you are giving a unit to someone else, the relationship between the superior and the subordinate persists. It is still in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, if I understand you well, a police unit is received by the military commander as attachment. That's an attachment. But the command structure is that of resubordination. But -- do you agree with that? That's the superior/subordinate chain of command that exists from the moment on that the police unit is attached to the military. Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Precisely. There was something else I omitted. It is only used for the duration of the task, following which it is no longer part of that formation. It is precisely as you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, this begs the question of whether a unit that is being transferred - and I'm using now the word "transferred" to use a neutral word - a police unit that is being temporarily transferred to the command of the army for a particular purpose, for a combat operation, and for a limited period of time, is it possible that during the time in which the police unit is taking part in the combat operation the authority over that unit could be split so as to say that in certain respects, for instance, in respect of the control of the activities of the police units at the front line, that this authority would fall under the commanding army officer's jurisdiction, while the units in other respects could still be under the authority of the MUP, such as, for instance, let's say as an example, criminal investigations and prosecutions for any possible crimes that were committed by the police unit during the time at the front line. Do you see my point? My -- my question to you is really: How strict do you describe the transfer of authority from the MUP to the army and back again? Because that is unclear. Either the army commander has full control, full and unlimited control in every respect over the police unit, or, given the circumstances, you may have situations where, actually, the army commander has control over the unit in certain respects, while the MUP retains control over the unit in some other respects. So, in other words, there is a partition, temporary partition of control over that unit. My question to you: Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the question. That is not possible. As of the moment the police unit is made part of the military formation, it temporarily loses its police authority. Their personnel are no longer authorised officials.
