They, in turn, become fighters, soldiers, under a single command. There's no parallel control or parallel command. That is also regulated in the army. There's no grey area there. As of the moment they are sent until the moment they returned to the police, they are under the competence and authority of the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand as much. And, of course, for the purpose of the fighting, for the combat activity, that's the way it has to be. The army commander must have the superior authority in respect of the combat activities, the fighting at the front line. But my question was really, rather, whether in some other non-combat-related activities the MUP could still retain a limited control over its policemen. And the example that I gave you was, for instance, criminal prosecution. Because, if I understood this correctly, and you may correct me if I'm wrong, but if I understood it correctly, the practical problem would very often be that the police unit would be attached or resubordinated to the army for such a short period that it would be impractical for the military police and the military courts to conduct the investigations, because, once these things were under way, the police unit would long since have been transferred back to the MUP. So it would make sense, perhaps, that, for activities of this kind, the authority would remain with the MUP so that it would be the civilian courts and the civilian investigators who would take over the investigations and possibly the prosecution of these people. So I -- I put my question to you again: Is it excluded in any circumstance that, as for the investigation and prosecution of crimes in certain conditions, the authority could be still falling under the MUP or under the civilian authorities, and not the military police and the military courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my opinion that it is not possible. As of the moment they are made part of the army, they are under the jurisdiction of Military Prosecutors and military courts. This is my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you also deal with the term of resubordination, as well as a number of other terms. Can you tell us briefly what seems to be the action and what seems to be the relationship with all these terms when we discuss recruitment, resubordination, attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation. What is the relationship; and what is the action?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be more precise this time around. When we talk about recruitment, attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation, all these, for the most part, are combat-related activities, save for co-operation. The relationship, I reiterate, is always, always, that of the singleness of command and the relationship superior/subordinate. There is an exception, though, which is co-operation. More frequently than not, it is in co-operation with civilian structures in the field, which means that the level of participation of all those involved is at the same level. It's a peer-to-peer relationship. In all other categories, the relationship of superior and subordinate is maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well? Resubordination, or, rather, recruitment, attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation -- sorry. Are what?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And resubordination?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the relationship in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, it may just be me, but I simply didn't understand that answer to Mr. Krgovic's question: Did I understand you well? Resubordination -- or, recruitment attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation are what? And the answer came: Co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, partially it was my mistake too. Recruitment, attachment, coordination, coordinated action and co-operation are what?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the activities, the actions; whereas, resubordination is the relationship. A regulated relationship of different parts within any given units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, that's what I wanted to ask you. In the rest of your report, particularly paragraph 216, you say that in a state of war, an imminent threat of war, and in other emergencies, the police may be used to carry out combat tasks of the armed forces in accordance with the law. The paragraph goes on to say: "While carrying out combat activities of the armed forces, the police shall be subordinated to the officer in charge of the combat operations." Let me ask you this: As part of the military doctrine, as well as practice and in terms of the law, can you explain to us why this is so? Why is the police subordinated to the officer in charge?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just read, Mr. Krgovic, is something that I took over from the Law on All People's Defence, specifically Article 104, as I stated in my report. What is highlighted here is that there is such a possibility and such possibility is allowed involving the use of police in the course of carrying out combat tasks, and, in my view, that should happen only exceptionally. However, in the second paragraph of this Article, it is decidedly and clearly and precisely stipulated that, if that happens, the police force will be subordinated to the officer in charge who is directing the combat operation. It seems to me that yesterday I spoke about this to a certain extent and that I said that this kind of legislature is fully justified because control and direction of combat operations is exclusively being studied at military schools and military academies and never at police academies. The police is trained to carry out different tasks. For that reason, the police is subordinated to the officer who is in charge of combat operations and who is trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 217, you speak about this relationship, and you said that, as of the moment they report to the officer in charge and the unit -- the whole unit will be resubordinated to the command of the unit that it is attached to and they become an integral part of the military structure. You started answering this question, though, but can you tell us again when exactly is this moment in time when they become military conscripts and until which time they retain that status that involves all the duties and responsibilities stemming from that status?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, I answered this question to the Honourable Chamber, but I'm going to repeat it. As of the moment when a unit leaves a public security station premises, that is the moment when their status of conscripts commences, provided this dispatch is regulated by a proper document. It will last until such time as the police members return back to their public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, could I just ask you here: When the police unit returns to its public security station, is that triggered by a written order by the army commander who releases officially the police unit? Or can the police unit return to their CSB or their SJB without any firmer -- without any further formal orders being issued. That is to say, once the combat activities are over, then they just go home. I mean -- so my question is: Does the return of the police unit back to its public security station require a written order by the army commander to release them; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, it is possible, in practice, that the document on the sending out of the unit already contains all the details concerning the duration of the tasks that they're going to perform. That's one way to do it. If the document only stipulates the detachment without stipulating the time-frame because sometimes you don't know how this was going to last, then a new document must be issued governing the return of this unit to the police station. It is not possible for such a unit to leave the front or the unit that it is attached to of their own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just as a follow-up to the question of Judge Harhoff. Can you tell us who issues this document on the termination of the need to have a specific police unit engaged in combat operations. In this second instance when you said that the original act does not stipulate the time-frame, who is the one who decides how long the need is going to last?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can be done by the commander to whom the unit was attached, and he reports on this to his superior commander, provided he had completed the task given to him by his commander. But a more proper way would be, and it would be in line with the rules, that the same entity that issues the document on the sending of the unit, the same entity would issue a document stipulating the return of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about a military commander?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exclusively a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. General, in your report, you spoke about -- I can see it in paragraph 218, that you speak about coordination. And you extensively explained this term "coordination," but you are putting it within the function of command and control. Can you tell us who is it who decides on coordination and draws up coordination plans, and can you give us more details about this?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Coordination is one of the functions of command. Once a decision is made by the commander, as of that moment, the planning of combat operations is being activated, and that's the first step and first function of command. Once the plan is finalised, then the second function of command is called organising. When an organisation on how the decision is going to be implemented, then we have co-operation as the third component of the command, and there is a fourth component as well, which involves direct orders in order to implement the commander's decision, and, finally, the fifth function involves control of what has been implemented. Now, why is coordination required? Combat operations are extremely complex. They involve a large number of participants. It becomes even more complicated the higher the level. Coordination is a broader term which ensures that all these elements within the combat deployment or between different forces participating in a task to cooperate -- but, rather, not cooperate, to function as best as possible during the execution of the task. Its ultimate purpose is -- and it is being resolved specifically through the plan of coordinated action which is a narrower term than coordination, is basically to avoid to have own forces be exposed to friendly fire, to put it simply. So one has to know when air force is going to be engaged, when anti-armour units are going to be engaged, artillery and infantry, and this is the purpose of coordinated action which is preceded by coordination, which is a broader term, and then we go to the stage of the coordinated action in order to conduct it properly. It happened during the civil war that some position of our army were targeted by our air force. And you see also that currently in Libya and during the NATO aggression of -- against Yugoslavia. We have instances of the so-called collateral damage. And that is the worse possible outcome of bad coordination and coordinated action and co-operation, particularly if a large-scale operation is involved that has huge numbers of participants and enormous fire-power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I will only ask you, since this is close to the end of the day and we're all tired, just to slow down a bit for the benefit of the interpreters. General, can you please look at paragraph 224 of your report. It deals with coordinated action, and you tackled the notion of coordinated action as a form of coordination and as a narrower term than coordination in your previous answer. Can you tell me this: If you have a situation where you have a number of units in a coordinated action with the purpose of completing a certain task, what relations exist between the units involved in a coordinated action and who commands these units in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is always the commander who commands all the units that are within his formation. I just said that a coordinated action is organised between various elements. It is the unit commander who approves the plan for a coordinated action, which contains such details as to who, or when, and with whom, in which area, and on which task is going to be engaged, as well as within which period of time they're going to act in coordination. And there can be no ambiguity there. In other words, it is always the commander, whether we talk about brigade, battalion, a corps, the one who directs combat operation, including a coordinated action as part of the execution of combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when we see a commander's order to execute a military operation, and he says, Carry out the task in coordinated action with MUP units, what relationship is there between these units in coordinated action and the command? Are these units subordinated to that command, these MUP units?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is -- that is -- this is the construction of the matter and that's a leading question. The proper question should have stopped -- it's a bit late now, but the proper question is: What is the relationship between those units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a leading question because if you look at the previous answer to my question, he said: I just want to clarify it. I have basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question was: When we see a commander's order to execute a military operation, and he says, Carry out the task in coordinated action with the MUP, what is the relationship between these units in coordinated action and the command. This is where the question should have stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the answer what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as I say, it is a bit late now, but given my objections yesterday and given that Mr. Krgovic knows that this is it the crux of the matter, that was most improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said as much. Could you please answer the question. What is the relationship between units in coordinated action? You provided an answer a short while ago. I just wanted additional clarification.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units in coordinated action carrying out combat tasks act together, and I repeat for the umpteenth time, that they are always under the command and control of one commander. We can't have two people in command. When I say, or when it is said "in coordinated action with," this only shows that there's some relationship between them, but they're always under the command of the one commander who leads the operation or that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which commander is that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is always the military commander. Depending on the particular case or the example, it can be a battalion commander, a brigade commander, corps commander, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, answering Judge Harhoff's question, you spoke about the authority to instigate proceedings against police officers who did something unlawful while they were acting in the -- as members of a unit acting with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us look at 1D00411 now, which is tab 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the 1st Krajina Corps Command, and we see that it's the forward command post. The date is October 1992. We see that the subject is the abandonment of positions by police members. We see to who it was sent, the Banja Luka CSB, and the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, as well as the 43rd Motorised Brigade. The commander, or somebody acting on his behalf, hereby informs these organisations about the following: "We have received the following telegram from the RS army Main Staff ..." And then he quotes: "We hereby inform you that Prijedor police units members have abandoned their position and fled back to their towns. "Immediately file criminal reports for each individual and undertake other measures to inform the public, publishing their names ..." And it goes on to say what else should be done. This -- the purpose of this document is information. Can you comment on the contents of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not correctly translated. [Overlapping speakers] ... not it's not [Overlapping speakers]. I just said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I don't know what was said before because what was said before had all the hallmarks of a leading question but it wasn't interpreted. Now what did Mr. Krgovic said before this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I heard -- I heard -- what I heard was: This is for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]... I apologise. I said abandonment of positions by police members, information. I just read what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not blaming the interpreters, and it may that be Mr. Krgovic is going very quickly, but today we've had real problems. The interpretation is well behind, and it makes it very difficult to object on what is coming as a leading question. So I would therefore ask that Mr. Krgovic slows down and there's always a pause before the General starts answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I read from the document, and you can see it yourself. Could you please provide a short comment about this document with regard to the authority to instigate certain actions?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this is an example that explains my position, as I put it to Judge Harhoff when he outlined what could happen. So what does this telegram say? Police members abandoned their combat task at a time when they were soldiers. The event in question happened in Prijedor, as far as I know, in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. As far as I know, there was a military court and Military Prosecutor's office with that command. With this document, the commander of the Main Staff orders -- and we can see that it contains a quotation; there are quotation marks. He orders that the corps command, whose responsibility it is, file criminal reports against some individuals. This document also shows that the corps commander informs the CSB in Banja Luka, from where these police officers were probably sent to carry out this combat task, and I believe that it was right to do so. All this corroborates my position; namely, that police officers, when they carry out combat tasks, that they're under the command of a military officer, and, by virtue of that fact, he has the authority to launch proceedings against them when they commit disciplinary offences, misdemeanours, or crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, you seem to suggest that this is General Talic's order to the Military Prosecutor and to the military police to file criminal reports and so on. However, the way it looks to me is that this is an instruction addressed to the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's what it looked like to me when I first saw it. But the punctuation clearly shows - and I'm referring to the colon and the quotation that follows in quotation marks - that this is a document that the commander of the Main Staff sent to the corps commander. And he tells him, We hereby inform you, and so on. And the commander of the Main Staff orders the corps commander to initiate proceedings. The corps commander only informs the CSB of this. The other interpretation would be possible if there were no quotation marks; in other words, if there were no quotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can point out that, in fact, if one looks at the original also there is an set of quotation marks in the second paragraph but not on the third, but those have been put in in the English translation for some unknown reason. Not that I think it's going to make much difference, but just so that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I can be of assistance. Your Honours, I note that the original has only two, one at the beginning, and one at the end. And that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, the whole document as precisely as the -- as the witness confirmed is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's sufficient, thank you, Mr. Zecevic, to simply point out that there is an error in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do agree with that. Thank you. I'm sorry, I was misunderstanding then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a little time left and then I'll return to what you discuss in your report. Paragraph 229. You speak about coordinated action of various elements of the combat disposition of a brigade. Then in paragraph 232, you speak about the coordinated action plan. My question is: The coordinated action plan and all the elements you listed here, are they included in the final document? The combat document.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coordinated action plan is part of a more comprehensive document, and that is the plan of combat activities. I have already explained why coordinated action is organised between various elements of the combat disposition of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished this topic and about to continue with another, so I think that we can finish for today. And, for the record, I may need another 30 to 40 minutes tomorrow, so I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to accord me some 20 minutes more than expected so I can finish my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment. And tomorrow, unless there is a change, we're in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
